reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: Characterised by recurrent groaning sounds produced during a prolonged expiration in sleep, often occurring in clusters
A typical event begins with a deep breath in, followed by a drawn-out expiration accompanied by a monotonous groaning or moaning vocalisation
It arises predominantly during REM sleep but can also occur in non-REM sleep
The sleeper is usually unaware, while the sound is disturbing to a bed partner and often prompts presentation
It is benign and, unlike snoring, occurs on expiration rather than inspiration
In current classification it is grouped with the sleep-related breathing disorders rather than the parasomnias
Polysomnography shows the characteristic slow breathing with a markedly prolonged expiration during the groaning episodes
reference.pathophysiology: Catathrenia reflects an abnormal breathing pattern during sleep in which expiration becomes greatly prolonged and airflow is vocalised against a partially adducted larynx, producing the groaning sound. The precise trigger is uncertain; a disturbance of the central control of respiratory rhythm during sleep, particularly in REM, and possibly upper-airway factors, have been proposed. It is generally regarded as benign, without an associated significant gas-exchange abnormality.
additionalDifferentials: Snoring, which is an inspiratory sound
Nocturnal stridor, for example in multiple system atrophy
Nocturnal moaning or expiratory sounds of another origin
additionalInvestigations: Bed-partner account and, where possible, an audio or video recording of the sounds
Video-polysomnography with sound recording to capture the expiratory groaning and its sleep stage
Assessment of the breathing pattern, showing prolonged expiration without significant desaturation
Screening for obstructive sleep apnoea as a comorbid or alternative cause
Neurological review if nocturnal stridor or seizures are being considered
redFlags: Inspiratory stridor or neurological features suggesting a condition such as multiple system atrophy
Significant oxygen desaturation indicating a sleep-related breathing disorder
Stereotyped vocalisation with other features suggesting nocturnal seizures
Excessive daytime sleepiness pointing to coexisting sleep apnoea
reference.prognosis: Catathrenia is benign with no known harmful consequences for the sleeper, but it tends to be persistent and its main impact is disturbance to a bed partner; response to treatment, including continuous positive airway pressure, is inconsistent.
pitfalls: Mistaking expiratory groaning for snoring or obstructive sleep apnoea
Overlooking nocturnal stridor, which can signal serious neurological disease
Confusing stereotyped nocturnal vocalisation with seizures
Offering firm promises of cure when the treatment response is variable
references: International Classification of Sleep Disorders, 3rd edition (ICSD-3)
Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine (Kryger, Roth, Dement)
management: Reassurance and explanation of the benign nature of the condition to the patient and bed partner
A trial of continuous positive airway pressure, recognising that the response is inconsistent
Identification and treatment of coexisting obstructive sleep apnoea
Consideration of a mandibular advancement device or ENT assessment where upper-airway factors are suspected
Confirmation of the diagnosis by video-polysomnography to exclude other sleep-related breathing disorders
Sleep-medicine follow-up given the tendency of the condition to persist
